newsitem.title: UK: Nobel Peace Prize left me with no time - 1995 winner.
newsitem.headline: Nobel Peace Prize left me with no time - 1995 winner.

text.p: Veteran anti-nuclear bomb campaigner Joseph Rotblat said on Friday that winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1995 had helped spread his pacifist message, but it had left him with little time to do new research.

"It's made a very big difference to my way of life... I have had so many engagements during the year it has affected my ability to do original work. I have much less time to think," Rotblat told Reuters in an interview.
"I've devoted myself to peace, but it has brought no peace to me," the 87-year-old Rotblat joked.
Rotblat said he had had to employ a full-time secretary just to handle the mail generated by the Peace Prize.
"It has almost affected my nature. Nowadays I have to reject four out of five invitations, which is very much against my nature," he said.
But he would not have changed anything. "On the whole, the balance is positive... I may be saying the same thing as before, but people pay much more attention now."
A nuclear physicist who helped to develop the first atom bomb, Rotblat left the Manhattan Project in Los Alamos, New Mexico, once Germany's defeat in World War Two seemed certain.

"I felt there was no need to make a bomb. The only reason I started in 1939 was to stop Hitler using it against us... The whole idea of making the bomb by us was that it should not be used," he said a year ago when his award was announced.
He helped found the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs with other scientists, and led the campaign against nuclear weapons from a cramped office in central London.
The $1 million in prize money that came with the Nobel Prize went to the cause, Rotblat said on Friday.
"I gave all my money to Pugwash. They give me travel expenses, and we can also use the Pugwash money for other people to travel to meetings."
Rotblat said the highlight of his year was his work for the Canberra Commission set up by the Australian government.

Its report was used by Australia in a successful effort to get the United Nations to adopt the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty in September, and Australia is now campaigning at the UN for a ban on the production of weapons-grade nuclear material.
Speaking as the 1996 award was announced, Rotblat said he would like ex-U.S. President Jimmy Carter's work for peace in Africa and the former Yugoslavia to be recognised.
Told that the award had gone to Bishop Carlos Belo and Jose Ramos-Horta for their fight for peace in East Timor, he said: "I didn't know the names but I think this is a very good thing."
